card.title: Grammar Master Mindmap — the whole of English grammar on one page

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: English grammar is one sentence-mechanics system with six branches — word classes, the 12-tense grid, agreement, voice, narration, modals/conditionals — plus a micro-zone layer of articles, prepositions, tags and fixed pairs that supplies most exam questions. Learn each branch as a machine, walk the error-scan in fixed order, and the whole syllabus compresses onto one revisable page.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
SENTENCE = SUBJECT + VERB + rest. Find the head pair first.
PASSIVE = object + be (same tense) + V3 (+ by agent).
BACKSHIFT = everything one step back (time, place, certainty).

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Memorising 30 disconnected 'chapters'. ✅ All of grammar is 6 branches off one trunk: the sentence.  ·  ❌ 'My team are winning' (institution sense). ✅ Collective noun as one unit → singular 'is'.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Revise by redrawing this map from memory once a week — active recall beats re-reading.  ·  Pair with Grammar Hacks (speed) and Notice/Formal-Informal Writing (applied formats).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: One sentence, all six branches: 'Yesterday, each of the players, who had trained hard, was given a medal by the captain.' — agreement (each...was), relative pronoun, tense (had trained), voice (was given), narration, modifiers.  ·  The tense grid in one breath: I write / I am writing / I have written / I have been writing — shift all four into past and future for 12.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'He told that he was ill.' ✅ 'told' needs a person: 'told ME that' / 'said that'.  ·  ❌ 'a university' / 'an hour' feels backwards. ✅ Sound decides: /yuː/ → 'a'; silent h → 'an'.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **How to use this:** grammar is one connected system, not 30 separate chapters. This mindmap is the central trunk (SENTENCE) with six branches — every exam question hangs off one of them. Revise by walking the branches, not by re-reading chapters.  ·  **CENTRAL NODE — THE SENTENCE:** every English sentence = SUBJECT + VERB + (OBJECT/COMPLEMENT) + (modifiers). Everything below is either how these parts CHANGE FORM (morphology) or how they COMBINE (syntax). If you can locate the subject and verb of any sentence, you can solve any grammar question.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Cross out of-phrases before choosing the verb.  ·  Backshift everything one step: time, place, certainty move together.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Redraw the full map from memory: trunk + 6 branches + 3 sub-nodes, one example each.  ·  Q2. Where does a question-tag error live on the map? (Micro-zones.)

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: This map is the index of the grammar section: every topic page hangs off one of its branches.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Six branches: parts of speech, tenses, agreement, voice, narration, modals/conditions.  ·  Micro-zones decide fill-in-the-blanks: articles, prepositions, tags, non-finites, pairs.  ·  Scan order for errors: agreement → tense → preposition → article → pronoun.  ·  Voice needs a transitive verb; state verbs never passivise.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Every grammar question is either morphology (form changes) or syntax (combination rules).  ·  The 12 tense cells are generated by two questions — WHEN (time) and HOW it sits in time (aspect).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Which two branches dominate NEB error-spotting? (Agreement + Tense.)

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A mindmap walk for 'spot the error': agreement ✓ → tense ✓ → preposition ✓ → article ✗ (found it).

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **BRANCH 1 — PARTS OF SPEECH (the 8 word classes):** Noun (common, proper, collective, abstract, material; countable vs uncountable), Pronoun (personal I/we/they, possessive mine/ours, reflexive myself, relative who/which/that, demonstrative this/those, indefinite each/everyone, interrogative who?/what?), Verb (transitive vs intransitive; state vs action; regular/irregular),…  ·  **BRANCH 1 sub-node — determiners:** articles a/an/the, quantifiers some/any/much/many/few/little, and the demonstrative/possessive words that sit before nouns. The article rules and quantifier choices generate a large share of fill-in-the-blank questions.  ·  **BRANCH 2 — TENSES (12-cell grid):** 3 times (past/present/future) × 4 aspects (simple/continuous/perfect/perfect continuous). Key cells: Simple Present = habits & universal truths ('The sun rises in the east'); Present Perfect = past action, present relevance ('I have finished'); Present Perfect Continuous = since/for duration ('has been raining since morning'); Past Perfect…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: CONDITIONALS: 1) if+present→will; 2) if+past→would; 3) if+had V3→would have V3.  ·  AGREEMENT: verb follows the HEAD noun; each/every = singular; or/nor → nearest subject.  ·  Universal truths don't backshift.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'If I would have known...'. ✅ Type 3: 'If I HAD known, I would have come.'  ·  If you can find the subject and verb, no question can hide from you.  ·  Aspect answers HOW the action sits in time; time answers WHEN.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Grammar rules are machines — feed the input, the output is fixed.  ·  were for all persons in Type 2 conditionals (formal).  ·  Sound, not spelling, decides a/an.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Walk the scan order; don't re-read hunting for 'feelings'.  ·  Label any newspaper sentence: subject, verb, object + word class of every remaining word.  ·  Write the 12-cell tense grid empty and fill one example per cell — from memory.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Convert: She said, 'I may visit tomorrow.' → (She said that she might visit the next day.)  ·  Passivise in three tenses: 'The chef prepares the meal.' → present/past/present perfect passive.  ·  Walk the error-scan on: 'One of my friend have gone to America last year.' (friends; has/went — agreement + tense).
